To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the relative work load (i.e., the % of the individual's VO2 max or Wmax) was a significantly more precise indicator than the absolute work load (i e., the number of watts) of the physiological and subjective stress in heavy exercise; 2) the relative work loads in % VO2max and % Wmax were closely correlated; and 3) the % Wmax was the most precise indicator of the physiological and the subjective stress in heavy ergometer exercise
the relative work load (expressed as % VO2 max or as % Wmax) was significantly correlated to the rate of perceived exertions (RPE) and heart rate, whereas absolute work load (in watts) was not.

the procedure of establishing relative workload on the basis of a subject's maximum mechanical power output (watts) is of value if a more precise setting of the workload is desirable when measurements are impracticable.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a methodological approach to exercise testing, which allows for the individual variation in working capacity, and which is based on the individual's maximal power output (W(max)), rather than on the maximal oxygen consumption (V(O2)max).
the study of the effects of exercise and physical activity on the cardiovascular system, with particular reference to the development of hypertension.
the effects of physical exercise on the cardiovascular system and the regulation of blood flow.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the method of expressing work load relative to the subject's maximal mechanical power (Wmax) is a valuable and precise alternative to the method of expressing the work load relative to maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max).
the relative work load is a better predictor of the cardiovascular and subjective responses than the absolute work load.
the use of relative work loads is superior to absolute work loads in the interpretation of exercise test data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the method of relative work load based on Wmax may be a useful procedure for establishing relative work load in heavy exercise when measurements of VO 2 are impractical or if an individual’s HR-work load relationship has been altered, as for example by medication.
the relative work load (expressed as a percent of the individual's Wmax) is a more precise indicator of the exercise load than the relative work load expressed as a percent of VO2max.

the relative work load, expressed as % VO2 max or as % Wmax, was a better indicator of the individual's physiological state than absolute exercise level, and that the latter was a better predictor of the former than the former of the latter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relative workload is a much better indicator of the physiological stress than the absolute workload.
the relative workload is more consistent than absolute workload, and it’s also more sensitive to changes.

the use of a relative workload (e.g., % VO2 max) can help to reduce individual variation in exercise testing and may be useful in situations where the measurement of oxygen consumption is not practical.
